answer.label: Copied by Washington — not composed by him
answer.authorName: A French Jesuit “Rules of Civility” maxim (trans. Francis Hawkins)
answer.authorDates: Composed c. 1595 at the Jesuit Collège de La Flèche; English translation by Francis Hawkins, c. 1640; copied by Washington c. 1744
answer.sourceLine: The wording is real and even in Washington’s own hand: it is Rule 56 of the “Rules of Civility & Decent Behaviour in Company and Conversation,” which the teenage Washington transcribed into his school notebook around 1744. But he did not write it. The maxim descends from a French Jesuit courtesy manual of c. 1595, Englished by Francis Hawkins about 1640 ↗. Washington was the copyist, not the author — which is why Snopes rates the attribution “Misattributed” ↗.

source.excerpt: 56th Associate yourself with Men of good Quality if you Esteem your own Reputation; for ’tis better to be alone than in bad Company.
trail: Wikisource preserves the full copybook: Rule 56 reads “Associate yourself with Men of good Quality if you Esteem your own Reputation; for ’tis better to be alone than in bad Company” ↗ — verbatim, in period spelling.

The Papers of George Washington ↗ trace the rules to a treatise composed c. 1595 by pupils of the French Jesuit Collège de La Flèche, translated into English by Francis Hawkins c. 1640, and merely “set as a task for the schoolboy Washington.”
Snopes ↗ rates the attribution “Misattributed,” noting Washington transcribed — but did not originate — the maxim.
source.excerptNote: Rule 56 as it appears in Washington’s manuscript, in the original 18th-century spelling. Today it is usually modernized to “Associate yourself with men of good quality if you esteem your own reputation, for it is better to be alone than in bad company.”

source.rightsNote: The wording is far older than any copyright: the maxim was composed c. 1595 and translated by Francis Hawkins c. 1640, and Washington’s manuscript copy dates to the 1740s. All of these are centuries before the 1931 U.S. threshold, so the text is firmly public domain.

author.metaLine: 1732–1799 · First U.S. president; copied the maxim as a schoolboy
author.bio: George Washington (1732–1799) commanded the Continental Army and became the first President of the United States. As a teenager, around 1744, he copied out 110 “Rules of Civility & Decent Behaviour” into his school notebook as a handwriting and character exercise — a set of maxims he inherited, not invented. Biographers have long treated the rules as formative for his conduct, which is exactly why the lines are so often misread today as Washington’s own aphorisms.

misattribution.heading: Why it’s tagged to Washington
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabricated quote — the words really are in Washington’s handwriting. But crediting him as their author gets the story wrong.

items.scope: As the author of the maxim
items.why: Washington transcribed Rule 56 as a schoolboy copying exercise; he did not compose it. Snopes rates it “Misattributed” ↗, noting the rules were “regularly used by school children of that era.”

The line is often clipped to just “It is better to be alone than in bad company” and pinned to Washington on quote sites — a fragment of Rule 56 detached from its French-maxim origin, as the Washington Papers ↗ make clear.

misattribution.truthLine: The true origin is a French Jesuit courtesy manual composed c. 1595 and translated into English by Francis Hawkins around 1640 ↗; Washington simply copied it out as a boy.

context.heading: A copybook, not a creed
lead: In the mid-1740s a Virginia schoolboy filled a notebook with 110 rules of good conduct. Rule 56 told him to keep good company. The exercise was ordinary for the period — the maxims had circulated in England for a century, and in France for a century and a half before that.
Because those rules seemed to describe the grown Washington so well, later admirers began quoting them as Washington. The sentiment fits him; the authorship does not.
detailsBody: c. 1595 — Pupils at the Jesuit Collège de La Flèche compile ‘Bienséance de la conversation entre les hommes.’
c. 1640 — Francis Hawkins publishes an English translation, which runs through many editions.
c. 1744 — An unknown hand selects and simplifies 110 rules; the teenage George Washington copies them into his school notebook, including Rule 56.
context.pull: The handwriting is his. The wisdom he borrowed.
